Stelle, throughout the entire time they had known each other, kept on telling him that everybody on Amphoreus needed a holiday, but apparently Phainon especially needed one. Something something something he had extreme trauma from reliving the same-ish 33 million gruelling cycles and falling in love again and again and again only to kill all those whom he loved again and again and again for that nigh impossible chance to stall the growth of Irontomb and figure out a way to stop the whole cosmos from imploding.

Phainon did not want to go on this “road trip” for a multitude of reasons. He did not need it, first of all. The anger and love alike in his heart were all that was needed to sustain him. He also had other things to do, such as spending time rebuilding Amphoreus, trying to hang out with his friends without thinking of their fresh corpses and destroying Nanook into less than atoms. Lastly (for now, this was hardly an exhaustive list) Phainon did not want to be babysat by some doctor named Ratio, of all the names.

But no, Stelle had used her backseat therapy skills to declare that Phainon desperately needed a change of scenery and of people. And then they used one of his only remaining weaknesses: his dearest friends.

Aglaea had given him her blessings and told him to enjoy himself, and then strong-armed him into accepting the Nameless’ invitation. After all, how could he or Amphoreus ever heal if he never took a well-deserved rest? She then quietly reminded him that the Nameless were honoured guests.

Anaxa looked him up and down, grimaced, rolled his eye, then clasped his shoulder in an awkward but well-meaning gesture and told him: “Just fucking go.”

Phainon sighed. It seemed that all of his friends agreed with Stelle's idea. Having all of his loved ones live out the rest of their lives in the light of a new dawn was certainly a balm on the soul, but having everyone gang up on him was a very devious tactic. He begrudgingly respected Stelle’s cunning.

Of course, the final nail on the coffin was Mydei, striding forward to give Phainon a piece of his mind.

“You have done well, Deliverer. You deserve a rest. Weak and tired as you are now, you won’t pose any challenge to me.”

And then Mydei smirked, eyes crinkling at the edges. Like every time Phainon was seen as worthy of such a sight, his breath stilled in respect for such beauty. (He always treasured Mydei’s smile and his glinting golden eyes; even dying, he always forced himself to watch as they dulled into bronze.)

“Unless you're scared of going into the great unknown?” Mydei drawled, both of them knowing that Phainon was not scared of that. Mydei's smirk softened at the edges, opening up into the smile Phainon knew was for him alone. Then he used the sharp edge of his gauntlets to cut off the eternal plait that always framed his face. Without it, he looked a bit naked, that key defining characteristic gone for the first time. The blunt strands flared at the edges. Mydei then placed the plait in his hands. Not even a block of gold could ever compare to the dusky sunrise of his hair.

“For your silly pendant,” Mydei said, brows furrowed in embarrassment rather than anger.

“Alright. I'll go… but I can't guarantee these millennia-old shoulders can ever be rejuvenated, so I’ll need a bath or two when I come back.”

Mydei rolled his eyes fondly, and soon Phainon left on the Astral Express to some city known as Pier Point.

When the express disembarked only a scant hour later, Stelle briefly described what Ratio looked like: purple hair, orange eyes, tall, muscular and had one hell of a gyatt. Phainon wasn’t sure what a ‘gyatt’ was, but he had a couple of suspicions.

He was a tall, surprisingly muscular man for a devoted scholar (he carefully tried not to compare his stature to a certain someone) and was wearing a stone plaster head. Well, Phainon had seen stranger things — wait, was up with his clothing? Even Aglaea would approve of the mixed draping fabrics that wouldn’t look out of place being sold in Okhema’s markets, and the very tight and revealing cloth underneath.

“Have I seen him before…?” He mused to himself. Stelle gave him a fierce side eye, clearly fearing that his mind had fully broken at that specific moment.

Like any trained soldier, he took a quick, assessing glance at his surroundings. It was completely different from the general aesthetics found in Amphoreus, all smooth lines and grand, echoing spaces with tiled walls so polished in texture he could see smudges of his reflection in them. Phainon, of course, expected the skies beyond Amphoreus to be different, but he was admittedly hung up on the lack of pillars. After a couple of millennia, the scenery and the bodies blended together in shades of gold and white. Everything had become so small. His purpose had narrowed into one goal, the Eternal land became nothing less than a landmass to him.

He should have been marvelling at the opportunity to witness something new, but he was just…drained. For a while, he was completely drained of everything: his memories, his millennia-old purpose, his fury. Now, he was woefully out of his depth in new territory. If he could fully transition from living as a country bumpkin to a hero, he could endure the sudden perspective shift for three days.

He chided himself for his senseless nerves; he was far too old for that. Besides, he dealt with feeling like a small fish in a large ocean time and time and time again (perhaps Amphoreus was more of a pond and Aedes Elysiae was more of a puddle—). Phainon consciously breathed in and out and in and out.

He focused on other things, such as Doctor Ratio striding towards him and Stelle.

“Ratio!” Stelle crowed, waving her hand around with the chaotic frenzy of an excitable chimera, nearly bashing Phainon’s head multiple times. With a slight grin that didn’t quite fit as well as it used to, Phainon waved his hand too, all too aware of how they were catching looks from everybody.

Ratio greeted her with an elegant marbled nod. “I’ve been told you’ve been unreachable ever since you reached the Eternal Land.” His voice changed to a steely register that gave Phainon flashbacks to his graduation(s). “Have you been doing your homework?”

With a nervous chuckle, Stelle patted him on the back before making her escape, somehow more scared of a scholar than the Titan of Death, Titan of the Skies, Titan of Strife, etc. Phainon understood immediately, and a rush of sympathy bloomed in the decrepit ruins of his charcoal heart.

“Hahahah, yeah, Phainon ate my homework when I got isekai’d as his childhood friend and snitched on him, but byeeeee! Great to see you again!”

For a singular second, Phainon mildly considered blowing her into smithereens. The second passed, and Phainon felt the urge to protect his honour in front of a scary scholar rise.

As if he weren’t a man who held onto his (dubious) sanity throughout 33 million iterations of all of his loved ones dying and then didn’t announce war on a whole ass aeon, Phainon awkwardly held out his hand, then hastily recalled that, hey, different planet, different customs, right?? Oh, may Kephale strike him down.

Ratio took his hand and shook it firmly. In his panic over trying not to implode, Phainon’s grip was weaker than a baby’s. Now he must seem like a dweeb, to use a certain traitor’s vernacular. He could practically hear his love laughing at him for his weak, cowardly grip. The completely unknown stranger did not laugh at him, just accepted the pathetic shake. He did not do much of anything, really. He was completely inscrutable due to his hidden face and because he never met him throughout 33 million cycles. Phainon did not intimately recognise the sound of his footsteps or how he would breathe out a laugh; Phainon did not know what he looked like dead.

Impatiently, Ratio gestured for Phainon to follow him. Directionless and lost, Phainon followed, thumbing the pendant as gently as he could.

Phainon couldn’t help but see the ghost of his loved ones everywhere he looked, but who could blame him? After all, he has been loving every single friend every single cycle with reckless abandon, even when his brain wished he could stop feeling, stop hurting every time he grabbed those golden coreflames from limp ribcages. Even in a whole different place, his love continues to pursue him like the scent of death and rot. It lingers, like how he sometimes can’t quite get blood out from underneath his fingernails.

He looked at Ratio, and all he could think about was his old professor. On the surface, they were quite alike (the cavity that once held the coreflames ached fiercely). They both walked and spoke like they could never quite have enough time, as if every breath could be spent on something else worthy of their attention. They both breathed and lived with some hidden schedule only they could make sense of. Maybe Phainon was projecting; Anaxa would be very disappointed in him. But as they paced over to Ratio’s car to start the road trip, Phainon took something akin to comfort in his blunt manner and sharp tongue and even sharper eyes.

As soon as they entered his car, his plaster head dissolved into nothing. Phainon drank in each feature to forcefully separate their conjoined images; it was unfair to Ratio to keep comparing him to somebody else that he may never meet. That, and Phainon really should have been paying attention to his words instead of surface-level similarities. Sometime after a couple thousand cycles, he could predict what each Chrysos Heir would say with 99% accuracy (he does not say 100% because Anaxa would rise even from the grave to give him another lesson on statistics and beat him up), which unfortunately gave him the bad habit of sometimes forgetting to tune back in with his ears. Of course, Phainon was planning on working on that minor issue.

The minute passed in awkward silence until Ratio made a pointed cough and glared at him. Unfortunately, his all too similar golden eyes make Phainon’s heart lurch in its rib cage until he employed all of his determination to absolutely nuke that feeling.

“My apologies, professor.” Is what slips out of Phainon’s mouth on instinct. It’s almost as embarrassing as the 33 million times Phainon accidentally called Anaxa ‘dad’.

Then Ratio huffs out a suggestion of a laugh, his previously stony countenance (shame that Hyacine or Castorice wasn’t there to laugh at his bad jokes) melting juuuuust a tad. Oh, thank goodness the horrors hadn’t taken away all of Phainon’s charisma.

“Professor? Well, I shall take that as a desire to learn from me, then.” Ratio dryly commented before turning on his car, tapping at a couple of screens until it started to rumble beneath both of them.

Thankfully, Phainon gained a crash course on some common things that were found in the wider cosmos, by courtesy of the Astral Express, so he gracefully handled his first car ride even as he wondered what on Kephale’s name prompted Stelle to describe this method of travelling as ‘dromas but with gears.’ It held absolutely no resemblance to a dromas, in Phainon’s humble opinion. It was far too steady and had a smell that wasn’t unpleasant but certainly wasn’t the (dubiously) fresh air of Pier Point. They started to move, and Phainon dutifully pointed out the traffic cones and lights to himself.

Ratio somehow manages to draw Phainon’s eye in the mirror whilst stuck behind a red light. “Do you require medical assistance for your arm?” Phainon tries very hard to figure out what he’s talking about. Ratio continues, “Pier Point Hospital’s prosthetics are top of the range.”

Oh yeah. Phainon stared at his stump. “Oh, there’s no need to worry, Professor. It’s a nice change of pace, y’know?”

The traffic light turned green, which meant he should be moving, but Ratio took a moment to do so. His face contorted in a wild flinch as he digested Phainon’s response. Any emotion was swiftly removed within the next second.

“Pardon?” He asked in a tone that Phainon had heard from Anaxa many, many times before, like that one time Phainon’s drunken escapades into writing real person fiction with Castorice about a certain professor got exposed. In every cycle but #12769, those sins were not found out by the muse of them.

“This is my first time with only one arm.”

Phainon gave him a somewhat innocent smile that probably suited him better before he got 33 million cycles dumped into his head, but he really had to work with what he got. Ratio pinched his nose bridge with such despair that even Phainon was impressed. After a deep sigh, he awakened a new man.

“Alright then,” he said, “would you mind if I invited somebody else on this trip?”

Ratio did not offer a reason, even after a beat of silence. Phainon wondered if he was going to hire a hitman or an emotional support being.

“No problem!” He replied, cautiously excited to meet another completely new face.

During another red light, the scholar quickly typed something on his phone and seemed to make a detour, suddenly driving left. He also turned off the mini screen depicting the path to follow.

“Don’t you need to use navigation to plot a new journey?” Phainon asked, applying his new knowledge about travelling in a car to make sure he could remember the details to share later.

Ratio’s mouth tightened at the edges. “... I’ve already memorised this particular path,” he admitted.

The air went weird from one-sided embarrassment; Phainon was slowly connecting the dots.

“Stelle mentioned that you were a highly renowned scholar.” he waited for an affirmation to continue, “I don’t know what she has mentioned about my planet’s background, but I lack knowledge of the cosmos’ Aeons and Paths.”

As he expected, any scholar worth their salt would be pleased with a student taking initiative.

“Normally, I would prefer for one to research such things on their own before asking, but considering your background, I shall make an exception. Is there any particular information you are seeking?”

“Thanks, Prof! I was thinking…” Phainon lost his weak smile and leaned forward, expression deathly still. “Do you know how to kill an aeon?”

“Why would you seek that information?” Ratio demanded with a straight face, nearly coming to a harsh stop in the middle of the road, which was maybe illegal or at least ill-advised. His next sentence was far quieter, his lips barely moving. “Now, this is highly sensitive information and you did not hear this from me, but only an Aeon can kill another, or through the collision of Paths.”

“Thank you,” Phainon whispered, mulling over the new information. So, if he wanted to destroy the Destruction, perhaps he should consider ascending to aeonhood to personally throw hands. He nodded to himself. But that raised another question: what would Phainon even become the aeon of?

In another hushed question, Phainon continued his interrogation, “How does one become an Aeon?”

“Talking about the known origins of the Aeons is hardly a controversial topic,” Ratio offered, now in his regular volume. Then, with a tone that truly suited lecture halls and debates, he regaled how Nanook ascended into aeonhood. Phainon focused on every word, internally losing his shit. Why would Ratio choose Nanook specifically, and why did he look like a local from Phainon’s homeworld?

As it turned out, Ratio did get an emotional support human in the shape of a handsome blond man wearing a vibrant shirt with a considerable amount of chest showing. Phainon wished he had his emotional support human in the shape of a handsome blond(ish) man wearing a vibrant shirt with a considerable amount of chest showing. Despite his envy, Phainon took a moment to appreciate the strange, saturated pink draconic birds on the stranger’s shirt.

Said man knocked on the driver’s window only a minute after Ratio stopped on the driveway to a sleek household that was reminiscent of the city’s train station, opulent and sanitised. Phainon stared at the incongruous marble statue that most certainly depicted the doctor he had just met. Maybe he should ask who the artist was so that Mydei’s graceful and otherworldly countenance could also be immortalised in the finest marble. Being so wrapped up in the image of a 60-foot Mydei statue, he completely missed Aventurine’s instinctual death stare at some hussy sitting at the back of Ratio’s car when Ratio invited him to a three-day holiday.

Once the new face settled into the seat beside Ratio, Phainon studied him, completely aware he was being studied in turn, lurid eyes swiftly catching the stump then returning to his face. He, as previously mentioned, was blond. But when the light behind him and his strands were backlit with faded gold, all Phainon could think about was Aglaea’s wavier, finer hair and her warm golden life essence spilling into golden water, dissipating into thin, fine threads—

The face changed from the immaculate veneer of a businessman with a polite yet oddly provoking smile to something confused. (Aglaea would not—) Then he reached awkwardly behind to offer a handshake, which was something Phainon could certainly do. He returned it automatically, blinking away the afterimages of her. It settled behind his eyelids anyway, like when one stared into the sun carried by Kephale’s straining shoulders.

“Hello, friend, I am Aventurine,” he said the title as if it were a threat, “of the—”

Ratio shot a glance at his partner and cleared his throat, stopping Aventurine in his tracks. “This is a holiday, Gambler, not a networking event.”

Awwww, they even had nicknames for each other! (Phainon did not know if he wanted to laugh or sob whenever he heard or even thought of Mydei’s nickname, a shackle, a testament to his dedication, an unwavering declaration of faith, all in one.) How cute!

“Y'know, Doc, I sure didn't expect you to be picking up strangers. Change of profession?” Aventurine joked, his gaze behind his pink sunglasses never leaving Phainon.

“I’m doing this as a favour from Stelle, but I invited you of my own accord,” Ratio gently corrected, and Phainon was a very awkward intruder trying his best to melt into the background. Then, resolutely looking at nothing but the road ahead, “You mentioned that you wanted a holiday, and certainly not in Penacony.”

Aventurine’s face froze, his teasing smile twitching like a dying fly. He murmured out, “How sweet of you, doc.” His weak attempt at playfulness was quite pitiful, but people trying to melt into the background did not draw attention to themselves, so he imagined what Mydei would say if he were subjected to such a scene.

Well, Mydei would say that Phainon was hardly better in the feelings or romance department. Oooh, self-burn. (Is that what a Self-Annihilator did? Phainon only had the hare-brained, no-context musings of the trailblazers to go off on.)

“So, Ratio, where are you taking us?” Aventurine’s expression smoothed out to pleasant, distant neutrality.

“The beach.” The scholar answered smoothly, only shooting a vaguely miffed look when Aventurine let out a playful laugh.

Aventurine’s grin was quite smug when he teased, “All that talk about taking adequate rest breaks throughout the week, but you have no idea what to do on a proper vacation, do you, doctor? You’re probably just following what those IPC travel pamphlets suggest, right?”

Ratio stayed conveniently silent.

“How long have you guys been together?” Phainon earnestly asked, watching their interactions as if it were one of those trashy flicks he liked to watch with Castorice on her (better quality, very pristine, not cracked at all) teleslate. Aventurine’s jaw closed with a quiet click.

Nobody spoke for the entirety of the car ride afterwards.

The beach was a novelty to Phainon, who was born and raised and re-born and re-raised in Aedes Elysiae, where the biggest body of water was more of a lake and then lived the majority of his life in the city, but unfortunately, it was a novelty he was having mixed feelings on. There weren’t many sandy places in Amphoreus, either, so the sensation of sand being everywhere, intruding upon every single millimetre of his skin, was not appreciated. However, the view was good, the limitless ocean crashing onto the coast, dragging wet sand backwards only to return it in the next motion.

Like Stelle and Dan Heng, he decided to take a couple of mementoes, taking a couple of photos, wincing at their blurriness. Well, at least his Teleslate still worked. When he showed off the photos to his friends, he’d likely have to defend his awful photography with vigour. Oh, Mydei would certainly make fun of him, and in turn, Phainon would demand a photography competition that would end with Mydei’s victories outnumbering his by one.

Like how the glass bottle containing a young boy’s wishes always drifted back to the craggly coast of Aedes Elysiae, Phainon’s thoughts would always reach out to Mydei, in slumber and in peace and in war and in death. This time, he wished Mydei could see a gentle ocean with warm currents and even warmer sand with no monsters lurking underneath. But then again, Mydei would find such scenery boring after a while. He’d take better pictures, though, eyes and hands trained from years of carefully curating his secret social media posts.

His eyesight naturally turned to the fresh disturbance. His new scholarly acquaintance rose out of the sea like an overly dramatic depiction of Mnestia gliding from the sea, torso bared and water glistening in the sun. Already having a solid idea of what to expect, Phainon observed how the blond man sunbathing on the sand was watching the sight with more focus than necessary. Phainon was certainly being far too nosy — he had only known them for several hours. Maybe it was precisely because of the minute timeframe he had known them that had driven him to such madness. They were very new to him, and every act they committed would be unknown to him because he had no idea who they were yet, which was beginning to culminate in a desire to push them together to see what disaster or miracle would bloom.

Ratio walked over to where Aventurine lay on a pristine beach chair, sprawled like a spider on its web, and leaned over to ask something. Phainon kicked at the water and watched as the droplets merged with the spume and air, feeling a bit like a lost toddler trying to amuse themselves. Well, a toddler could be occupied by anything and everything, their buoyant hearts and imagination waiting for even the smallest bit of kindling. Alas, Phainon did not have such energy at that moment.

Phainon still doesn’t understand what was supposed to be relaxing about the beach — was he supposed to watch the endless swash and backwash of the ocean 33 million times?

He shifted his feet in the coarse sand, grounding himself in the tickling sensation of grains smoothing below the sole of his feet. He soon had an idea for some proper relaxation and was almost disturbed by how obvious the idea was.

Quickly, the shifting susurrus of the sand alerted him to Ratio’s presence.

“Hello,” Phainon greeted, “is there anything I can do for you?”

“No. What would you like to eat? Something more familiar to you or something different entirely? It’s currently lunchtime.”

“Ah, thank you, but I don’t need—”

His rebuttal was cut harshly by the sharp, mildly disappointed look that reminded him far too much of Anaxa. Like the overly sensitive plant Phainon had inadvertently killed 33 million times over, Phainon wilted.

“Yes, Prof.” His mind scrambled to find something that should be easy to find, he’d like to eat, even when he no longer required such sustenance. What would be easy to find in Pier Point? He’d forgotten what it felt like to be a complete stranger to an unknown land by now, unsettled by the initial discomfort of not knowing the streets and houses like the palm of his hand.

Eyes sharpened in focus, Ratio pondered on what to do with the buffering man in front of him.

“I’m having fried sea bass and coconut rice from a restaurant nearby. I’ve had it before and can vouch for its quality.”

“That sounds great, thank you!” Phainon said on instinct; his mother hadn’t raised him with bad manners, after all, even if he had fumbled a bit hours before. With a strained chuckle, he admitted he still did not have any cosmic currency except for one (1) singular credit courtesy of Stelle, but tried to sneak a gold coin into Ratio’s pockets the moment he turned around.

Ratio dodged each attempt without breaking a sweat, almost unnervingly unbothered. “There is no need to repay me.”

“Please, Professor! It’s a cultural thing, I absolutely cannot allow myself to mooch off of you!”

Somehow sensing Phainon’s lies like an overpowered chimera trained to sniff out dishonesty and trickery, Ratio raised a brow, and his expression conveyed that he wanted no further objections. “Somebody has already beaten you in your unnecessary race to pay. Bye.”

“Uhm, bye!”

Phainon vowed to sneak 100 gold coins into Ratio’s bag. Somehow. He didn’t even have 5 gold coins to his name, actually. He was broke as fuck, to put it mildly.

Rather than dwelling on his unfortunate financial situation (and all of the impulsive purchases of historical phonies that created such a situation), Phainon summoned his greatsword and went through his simpler sword moves, taking his time to adjust the motions for just one arm. In the heat of battle, he figured such things out on the fly, powered by millennia of accumulated battle prowess and sheer wrath. Now, he could afford to take things a bit slower and more smoothly.

The new terrain pulled him from the past — Phainon didn’t know how he had never trained his swordsmanship in the sand before, but the divots of sand he left in his wake were satisfying. Grains flew from the ground with each swing, the surface of the ocean rippled, and its foam sliced briefly, reforming within the next second. In his violent meditation, all thoughts and doubts and hatred were rendered null; perhaps conflict was the only thing he’d ever truly understand. Sparring with his lover, however, was always fun. (Well, until Mydeimos was nothing more than a titan with a coveted coreflame to the dawn-denied one).

He breathed out, let the fine salty mist settle in his lungs, and continued until his mundane form worked up a sweat. In the presence of guests, Phainon thought it would be rude to lose himself completely, so he released his greatsword and started his stretches with a tempered, ritualistic focus. He sought out the movement of his muscles and his lungs. He took a quick dunk in the water, nerves alight with the brutal coolness.

Once he was presentable, he decided to talk to his mysterious companion. Considering how those bejewelled eyes hadn’t left his direction, Phainon guessed it would be the right choice. Phainon may have only been in Aventurine’s presence for less than a day, but his sharp, assessing gaze hidden by a pretty, unassuming face reminded him of Aglaea. He swears it isn’t just because they were both blonde.

They both greeted each other as he came closer to the wooden chairs and he was quite glad that greetings across the cosmos seemed to be similar: a smile and a nod and meandering small talk. Hovering like some awkward fly, Phainon tapped his fingers against the chair’s arm as if trying to flick away the flaky remnants of the gold that plagued him constantly.

“Greatswords are quite an uncommon choice,” Aventurine commented, his mirrored sunglasses (a fashion fad that never stuck in Okhema, much to his disappointment. Aglaea would never let him wear them in peace.) glinting like a sword’s edge.

“They’re pretty popular in my world,” Phainon replied, despairing at his flaky, traitorous charisma.

“You use it like an extension of your own body.”

“Yeah, I’ve been practising swordsmanship for a long, long time.”

For a blistering moment, Phainon wished for whatever passing Aeon around to smite him to the ground; to think that everybody used to agree he talked too much.

“You know,” Phainon said with a smile that almost felt natural, “I could teach you.”

Aventurine barked out a harsh laugh, nearly choking on his water. “Good heavens,” he muttered raspily, then smoothed out his face and voice, “friend, I’m certainly not a warrior nor do I have the strength to swing it around even once.”

Phainon chuckled lightly, knowing damn well that whilst Aventurine might not be the picture of heroism (neither was he — that title belonged to Mydei, of course), he was certain that Aventurine was stronger than he seemed and had spilt blood numerous times and wouldn’t hesitate to do it again if necessary. Something in those battle-weary eyes of his that mirrored his own. Or maybe he was just projecting. Again.

Luckily, Ratio finally made it back, a large bag carrying all the containers, sitting down at the foot of Aventurine’s beach chair. Phainon eagerly dug in, pausing when he tasted unfamiliar spices. Ultimately, they were good, and he had never been a picky eater, so he continued to eat, albeit with tastebuds that were very confused from trying something new after eating the same-ish cuisine for a long time.

“I have a question,” Phainon said after a pause.

“Do go on.” Ratio replied, still eating at his own pace. Phainon noted that Aventurine was a far quicker eater than he was.

“What’s Pier Point like? And the food here, too? The fish was as good as you said it would be, Prof, thank you!”

Ratio offered nothing else but, “Aventurine has stayed here far longer than I have. He’ll likely have the answers you are looking for.”

“Well, thanks for the vote of confidence, Ratio.” Behind his glasses, Aventurine narrowed his eyes in confusion. “You want to know that? Well, I’m no Ratio but… well, this place is the headquarters of the IPC. Most of the people living here are IPC employers, including me. As Ratio also works under the IPC sometimes, he was given an apartment here. Not much to say about the food here, most things from the wider cosmos can be found here. There are restaurants here, too, of course, like the Kiliro Fish Restaurant that Ratio just went to. Most eat at restaurants after work; the lunch break's usually too short.”

After a pause, he then added, “I can go even further in depth if you want.”

Phainon shook his head, “Ah, no need, my curiosity has been sated! It’s always cool to learn how food culture differs from region to region.”

Ratio nodded thoughtfully, “Willing to share any examples?”

“For starters, I'm what's called a country bumpkin.” Phainon waited to see if that term was used or at least understandable; from the twitch of a smile from his audience, Phainon guessed it was. “I grew up in the rural countryside of Aedes Elysiae. There wasn’t a sea of flowers or even a sea in general, but there was a sea of wheat every harvest season. When I had to move away to the city, I remember being strangely surprised by the different food, especially the dromas steak.”

As a generally good conversationalist when he wasn't planning on being antagonistic, Aventurine picked up the line of inquiry. “A dromas? I haven't heard that one before.”

As if the spirit of The Great Performer Anaxa, the infamous Dromas Draped in Finery, was looming over him with his pistol pointing right at his skull, Phainon tried to pay homage to the humble and amazing and the menacing four-legged beast. Judging from the carefully blank face from his main target (he had taken off his sunglasses, either to convey judgement or scrutiny or even to focus better), Aventurine was very much not understanding his description of a very gentle, but honestly very viscous beast the size of an average house — ok, so smaller than the apartments I see around here, so picture a very big lizard but with longer legs, like that of an ancient tree, they have tails like a lizard, too, but they do not move in a lizard fashion, they are the type of beast that bumbles around more than scurries — imagine such a beast scurrying around the streets of Okhema!

Aventurine summoned a coin made of Imaginary, then twirled it around his fingers and reached behind Phainon’s head.

“Is this your card?”

Aventurine flicked out a faintly glowing card, dark brown with tasteful streams of gold. He grinned, summoning others to form a fan, then revealed the pictures on the back: an extremely fucked up komodo dragon-esque creature with sharp fangs. Phainon, for the first time in far too long, broke into a peal of laughter.

“But seriously,” Aventurine dramatically complained, “your description makes no sense!”

From then, they worked on the depiction of what could be politely described as an unfortunate dromas-chimera that went horribly wrong, Phainon quickly describing the features that were entirely missing, such as their vivid colouring, ranging from purple to blue, and their patterning.

Aventurine gave them a most awful puce colour, one evocative of dreadful illness and despair. “Well, the living ones have a bit more colour in them, but it’s a great start!” Aventurine shuffled the cards, now showing off a colour that no gentle thing in the wilds could naturally produce. “Well, they are the colour of twilight, the gentle bridge between the night and day, a holy beacon guiding humanity forward.” Aventurine's smile widened. The next card’s dromas looked like Kokopo III in terms of colour and ferocity, but nothing else.

They continued the game until they hit a rut, in which Phainon could no longer help Aventurine beyond a vague ‘the white spots are less like weird pimples, more like little rocks embedded in them’. Even Phainon was beginning to lose hope; he was beginning to worry that his inability to praise the humble and wise dromas would somehow be sniffed out by Anaxa within a minute of them meeting again.

With the most exasperated yet stony expression Phainon had ever seen, Ratio created a perfect depiction of a dromas, complete with gentle eyes, their stubby little toenails Phainon kept on forgetting to mention, their funny little rocky eyebrows and a wagging tail. Its proportions were perfect. Their scales were perfect. As if nothing had happened, Ratio took a sip of his water.

What the [Aedes Elysiae expletive]

“We’re going to Pier Point Museum.” Ratio stated as he ushered them into his car again, and Phainon knew there was no other option; not that he was complaining, as he was pretty eager to learn about history in other worlds now that he had time.

Aventurine hummed in thought, turned again to Ratio. “I heard the monthly exhibit is on the Swarm Disaster, wanna go check it out?” As expected, the latter part was directed to Ratio.

“Of course,” the doctor replied as if there was no other option, “but if the quality is anything like last month’s exhibit, then I will be sorely disappointed.”

“You’re never going to let go of that, are you?” Aventurine said softly, lips curved ever so gently upwards.

Ratio huffed in amusement before diving into a short explanation of the Swarm Disaster and the Aeon of Propagation.

Phainon was heavily debating whether to ask hey, so how often do you guys go on dates to the museum and hey, could Mydei and I come along next time for a double date that would hopefully pull both of your heads out of your asses but as he did not want to make the atmosphere strange again, he kept mum — not because he had nothing to say, but because he was plotting. Scheming, even. They (the other Chrysos Heirs) may jokingly call him the son of a divorced couple, but that was not going to stop Phainon from making a couple out of them, no matter how hard it may be! If there was one thing Phainon knew, it was the indomitable human spirit and Mydei’s fantastic tits.

No, this was not him avoiding his own issues by distraction. He just had to repeat that enough times to fully believe it.

It seemed that one of the constants of the unfeeling universe was the cycle of destruction-survival-reconstruction-destruction of societies and worlds. Even the singular planet of Amphoreus was no stranger to the complete annihilation of the more unfortunate cities, until there was only one left. Aedes Elysiae, Dolos, The Grove of Epiphany, Aidonia were all left as mere bones of themselves. And then reset again and again—

Phainon hadn’t accounted for the sheer number of extinct planets and peoples across the cosmos. To think that a singular Aeon could account for such death, to think that Tayzzyronth was stopped only by several other Aeons. Humanity never seemed so unbearably small. However, Phainon was standing in Pier Point and was very much alive. Not even the Swarm could fully decimate the cosmos, and even Amber Eras later, there were still remnants of the fallen civilisations.

Behind the thin glass, a pair of shoes, weathered and clearly handmade, were placed on display. During the Swarm Disaster, there were records of a mother who, grieving her children, tried to have the bugs wear shoes. She failed.

A soft, mourning breath later, Phainon wrenched his gaze from that particular exhibit, absently appraising the other objects in that particular room: dinner plates, blankets, mugs, chairs, a doll. The Swarm had been hunting for food in their mindless propagation, and so the non-edible objects like the dinner plates were left mostly undamaged, and if they were not intact, it was because of the owners dropping or cracking them in their haste to evacuate. The blankets were left half-eaten, for when the bugs recognised that it wouldn’t provide them with the nutrition they were searching for, it was already too late.

If he concentrated, he could hear the distant hum of the professor and the businessman’s conversation. Glancing only slightly to the side, he saw that Ratio was likely delivering another lecture, this time to his situationship. Whilst he was grateful for the plethora of information Ratio had willingly given him, he also needed some time alone to absorb everything. Also, why would anyone in their right mind measure time with Amber Eras, aka whenever Qlipoth dropped their hammer. Like, where was the regularity?! Ratio was a kindred spirit in that aspect, at least.) The universe was wild. And quite desolate and depressing, but, most importantly, full of love and hope. That last part was very important to remember.

(Amphoreus was a dying land pulsing with a bitter, tenuous hope that may have frayed but never broke completely. And if a hero could be described as the beating heart of the city, Phainon gripped onto that thread, that singular vein, until the storm had finally passed.)

He stared at the portrait of the Sand King, the Aeon of Propagation. To become so lonely and bitter that you ascend from the sheer grief, becoming a shell filled with a cosmic hatred that burned. (His shoulder blades itched; the ripped seams of his useless wings itched.)

“Friend, you don’t look so good.”

Phainon let out a choppy breath, instinctual flex of his right hand rendered null due to it not existing anymore — not that it stopped him from feeling it. He turned around, where Aventurine lurked several metres away.

“I’m fine,” he lied.

Aventurine’s all too suspicious and knowing gaze travelled up and down his face, taking in the trembling pupils and trembling mouth. His gaze dared him to lie further.

Phainon rescinded his earlier words; he might as well give him something, even if no words could quite capture the fury and disgust trembling through his nerves. “It’s just… There's so much grief in the world. I hoped that my homeworld was the exception, one of the only planets to suffer from so many lost cities.”

Aventurine’s eyes also lingered on the Sand King, the copies of a once-extinct species congregating in such a dense swarm that they became one entity. “I’m afraid the universe is as inherently unjust as you feared.”

His eyes glistened like the carapace of a beetle, vivid and damp colours colliding into each other, an old, bone-deep tiredness and apathy threatening to spill over. Then Aventurine put his sunglasses back on and walked into the next room, and the illusion was shattered. Phainon sought out Ratio, only to find him to his left, observing the little boots. The museum wasn’t too busy at that hour: it was 3:30 on a Monday. He and Ratio were the only ones in the section. He mulled over the blond's parting words for a moment.

Keeping his voice low, Phainon said, “You and Aventurine sure are close.”

Of course, Ratio neither confirmed nor denied anything, knowing that Phainon had already observed enough homoerotic moments that it would be foolish to downplay anything. His shoulders were tense.

“I’m not saying this in a threatening way,” Phainon whispered awkwardly, rubbing his neck, “I just think he likes you back. Maybe you could, I don’t know, make a move?”

Ratio’s eyebrows furrowed in distaste. “Do you often insert yourself into private matters?”

“Honestly, no, but this trip has been fuelled by so much romantic tension I think it’s polluting the air.” In order to appeal to his emotions, Phainon twisted his face into the dreaded puppy eyes. His words were tinged with a sad, pathetic hint of a whine. “Please. I’m so tired of being the third wheel.”

Ratio’s eyes twitched dangerously, and the next moment Phainon was looking at that marble bust, but the doctor’s embarrassed discomfort was clear despite that barrier, arms crossed at his chest and shoulders hunched in.

“Y—You!” Ratio snapped, then hushed his voice into a deadly hiss. “It does not matter what I feel; I refuse to put him under any pressure! I would hate to act like those dreadful people from his past—”

Ratio released a harsh breath, shoulders rising only to fall like the snap of a guillotine; Phainon honed into the Implications and the drama like a honing missile — or, should he say, like the Lance of Fury. Ok, ok, ok. It seemed that Ratio would rather die than make the first move. (Mood, as the youth said.) Obviously, that meant that Phainon should pressure Aventurine instead, and he felt little guilt over it as he knew what had to be done.

“My apologies, I won’t bring this up again,” Phainon earnestly lied, mentally adding in a not with you, anyway, “I suppose that I’m too much of a romantic, but that was hardly polite… I pushed too much, didn’t I? I'm sorry.”

"Stop your unnecessary apologies." Ratio sighed deeply through that plaster bust. “I expect you to keep to your word, Phainon. Now move along; the next area is sure not to disappoint.”

Phainon let himself be ushered into the hallway by a disappointed Ratio, now feeling mildly guilty.

Phainon had to carefully keep the grin off his face as the three of them finally emerged from the gift shop. If it were his regular, sunny grin that he’d carefully curated over his years, he wouldn’t care. Unfortunately, ever since that stint of going absolutely maniacal with rage, he had found it harder to keep such chaotic energy to himself. The beginning of a proper plan was taking place, not that it was particularly complex. In fact, it was just the standard move of watching a horror movie with your crush, acting big and strong and then comforting your crush. Now this move only had a chance of working if: you were not squeamish and if your crush was squeamish. Yes, Phainon had tried it out with Mydei. No, it did not work as well as he hoped. Mind you, even Phainon of cycle #1149803 knew it was a stupid plan, yet persisted anyway.

His very awkward, very stilted invitation to Mydei about watching the newest horror movie, Scary Film 3, together was overheard by Hyacine and Castorice, and Phainon would hate to exclude them, especially considering how hopeful the two were. Alas, nobody but Little Ica enjoyed the movie, and that was a dubious statement to make considering Mydei had given him a handmade cookie and tenderly handfed him with a smile lit up from the gratuitous blood shed on screen. If he were Little Ica, he'd be in an exuberant mood for a whole week. Hyacine herself hadn't enjoyed the movie due to its medical inaccuracy.

“Personally, I think that the protagonist would have passed out from blood loss or shock long before going along with that silly deal of cutting off a leg to get out of the maze.” Hyacine poked at her companion's cheeks before adding, “Not to be rude, but the practical effects like the arterial blood spray and the third-degree burns were underwhelming.”

Mydei was unbothered by the egregious violence and summed up his thoughts in two simple words: beyond stupid. Of course, Phainon agreed, not just because he had little self-respect and could be quite the people pleaser at times, but mostly because the plot really was beyond stupid.

During the movie, Castorice had sat in the back, to the very left on account of her deathly (sweet!) aura. Thankfully, she mentioned that she was simply happy to be included, even when they were all watching something so stupid it would burn off Anaxa's remaining hairline from sheer rage. Phainon, however, noticed that she carefully did not mention her own opinion on the movie, and he had the suspicion she also found it uninspiring, given that she brought out her secret poetry notebook only a quarter of the way in. He even spotted his and Mydei's names several times!

When questioned privately about the matter, her pale face erupted in such vivid crimson that Phainon #1149803 never brought up the subject again in fear of her kicking the bucket from all her blood flow travelling to her face in one second.

Yet again, he got lost in the copious beloved memories, which was an improvement from the not-so-wholesome torrent that also plagued him, but also just as much of a nuisance in day-to-day life when Phainon was arguably free from his… everything. It's peace time, he told himself until it stuck. He instinctively felt somebody looking at him, only a side glance showing that it was just the doctor.

“Hey, Prof.” Phainon greeted, plastering on a smile.

“You've been staring at these fridge magnets for seven and a half minutes now,” Ratio commented mildly, but thankfully, he was no longer mad at him for prying. Well, it was mild for him, anyway, as his resting bitch face and tone made him seem far more aggressive than he actually was. Yet again, the images of similar people burned their images into his head like how the sun's afterimage bloomed with every blink.

“And you've staring at me with absolutely no thoughts between your thick head for roughly one minute,” Ratio commented, this time less mildly but more amused.

Phainon laughed awkwardly. “My bad. I, I was just looking at these little magnets. They seem pretty popular?”

“Indeed. Fridge magnets are generally considered a timeless gift that suits both friends, foes and annoying colleagues. Especially in this star system.”

Phainon snuck another glance at the board, all of them sporting the same font that was far too bold for something so ugly. In a harmony of pure ugliness, they all screamed PIER POINT MUSEUM with the enthusiasm of the tortured souls right by the River of Souls. Looking at the differing colour schemes, Phainon scanned each of them carefully (purple and white, navy blue and gold, pure gold, mint greens and pink…); they were of good quality and likely good material, judging by the satisfying weight of each one. But, of course, there was a bigger problem.

As if Zagreus themselves had blessed him, Aventurine seemed to sniff out whenever somebody was in need of money.

“It's on me,” Aventurine sang out with the usual levity, plucking the magnet Phainon was holding with such grace that Phainon did not feel even an iota of annoyance. Somehow, he picked the one that Phainon had been looking at. So flummoxed by that strange bout of luck, he protested far too late, and Aventurine was already running off into the counter. Ratio watched with something like pity, perhaps, as if he had been the unwilling participant of a reverse-scheme many times before.

After grabbing some more food that Ratio deemed a 'nutritional wasteland' and Aventurine a 'little bite of unholy delight', they stopped before the most colourful, swanky clothes shop he had ever seen. He gasped in delight — would they have orange pants?! He very much needed them after Aglaea burned them with all the Chrysos Heirs as witnesses. Aventurine winked at him when he turned around with the sheer chaotic energy of a hyperactive toddler. Ratio closed his eyes, looking upward, as if seeking advice from the cosmos itself or trying to look for his ever elusive patience.

“Is this where you got that pinnacle of fashion?” Phainon demanded eagerly, pointing at the dapper, fluorescent pink birds with strangely long legs.

"Sure is~" he sang out, grabbing the sleeve and pushing the hero of Amphoreus with far greater power than expected of such a slight figure. Impressed, Phainon let himself be herded like livestock to the fancy, bright boutique. (Was there a difference between that and a regular shop? Hm, something to consider later.)

"Absolutely not," Ratio retorted, not even bothering to open his eyes to witness the foolish shenanigans the two had gotten themselves involved in.

Phainon gave the absurdly bright tropical shirt a mourning look; Aventurine refused to give up.

"Come on, doc! It'll be fun!" Aventurine crowed like the nuisance he was. "You will match with us."

After a beat of silence, he sighed deeply in defeat and fled, shooting the Kremnoan hand signal for attack towards the warrior. Phainon warmed his expression in idle curiosity and showed off the silent wonder that had been tailing him throughout his entire journey. Whilst this tactic may not have worked on Anaxa well, it was the perfect bait for a professor like Dr. Ratio, whose sole goal in life was to disseminate the world's knowledge onto the foolish and dull. Or something. This was all Aventurine's plan.

"The birds in my homeland are quite dull in comparison to these flamingos." Phainon's voice tripped up on such an unfamiliar, albeit fun, word. "Your friend said something about its colour being a product of its environment…?"

As if a sleeper agent's codeword had been activated, Ratio's golden eyes snapped open, and Phainon was quite happily held captive in a lecture on how that bird's diet influenced their brilliant pink feathers. Ratio even showed some pictures of them, and Phainon was entranced by their absurdly long legs— he initially thought the dapper patterns had over-emphasised their scaly legs. The professor then showed a devastatingly endearing photo of a baby flamingo.

During that exchange, Aventurine had successfully brought all three shirts and lurked behind Ratio, waiting for the right moment to pounce. Even Phainon was impressed by his silent approach. However, just as Aventurine was in arm's length, whatever radar the professor had cultivated to sniff out nearby idiocy blared, sharpened into a wonder of nature after years of accompanying a certain fool on his even more foolish escapades. He sighed deeply and pinched the bridge of his nose to ward off an incoming headache.

"What have you done now?" Ratio demanded weakly, seemingly already submitting to his fate.

In response, Aventurine ushered the gift bag into his arms with a subtle laugh, which also seemed to be the final push to win against Ratio's defences. Reluctantly, he accepted the gift.

After all of the junk food Phainon had tried out, Ratio had ordered him to try out the fruits and vegetables from the market, a scant 15-minute walk away from the boutique.

"The apples from my homeworld are better," Phainon accidentally let slip out.

Ratio sighed longingly. "Unsurprising." Phainon shot a suspicious glance at him, still unsure whether that was an admission that the scholar was, indeed, from Amphoreus. Phainon let the suspicions drop.

Soon, he noticed that their group held a slightly awkward vibe when eating together. The Chrysos Heirs would often feast with each other, sharing honey mead and something Mydei made, sometimes after a successful exhibition, sometimes after a festival, sometimes for no reason at all. Given how his two companions consciously did not look at each other whilst eating or put far too much thought into their looks while eating, Phainon had his suspicions that they did not eat together often. If their relationship were to progress any further, they had to eat together — or eat each other, even. Heh.

Of course, there was the likelihood that it was Phainon's presence making things more awkward, which only meant that he had to give them the illusion of privacy at some point. Indeed, a fine plan. Phainon was going to get such a good score in matchmaking, which was a totally normal thing to yearn for. If Anaxa were to suddenly create a matchmaking course and teach it, Phainon would totally graduate with honours.

(Of course, Anaxa would never make such a thing, as it would involve too much self-reflection on his absolute failure of a love life, which was really ironic given that he was semi-involved with the demigod of Romance — ouch, Phainon got a bit aggressive there hahahah.

Throughout all of the cycles, there was always something going on between the two, but Phainon only realised it was something other than pure hatred until Cycle #169, in which he had killed the both of them together, only to witness his teacher kiss her with tongue, only to promptly explode himself straight afterwards in an attempt to take Khaslana down with him. His golden blood had stained her pure white dress. That was one wild cycle.)

"Heyyyy," Aventurine called out, looking as if he were ten seconds away from snapping his fingers in his eyesight to gain Phainon's attention and annoyance.

"Sorry, did you say something?"

Aventurine waved off his apology, "Where are you staying tonight? Did Stelle book you a place?"

"She did, just let me—" he brought out his phone, scrolling through the very incriminating messages Stelle had sent that evening (such as the waves of photographs lovingly rendered by March 7th's camera, all depicting Mydei and his peerless beauty.) Aventurine looked respectfully at his beauty; Ratio was admiring his peerless muscles, and Phainon angled the screen away.)

"This place." He said, not even attempting to pronounce the flowery name.

Aventurine's eyes narrowed in focus, then sneered. "Oh, ew, not on my watch." Then Aventurine flipped a coin. When it landed on tails, he gave a considering hum. Ratio called him an idiot. "Are you good with pets?"

Phainon gasped with such delight that he almost felt rejuvenated. He hastily flicked through his picture album (scrolling past albums such as: Mydei I, Mydei II, Mydei III, Mydei IV, Mydei V. The last had a black screen as the album picture), eventually scrolling into Awooooo Firm! with each photo comprised of the little gremlins Hyacine watched over.

Aventurine took his phone, scrolling past the dense images with the ruthless focus of a true businessman, or rather a fastidious judge. He handed them back with a nod, and Phainon remembered the time in which Kokopo III finally accepted his offerings of premium sand and love after years of biting him for the sole crime of existing.

"Doc, do you want to join us for a sleepover at my place?"

Ratio considered it. "Perhaps another time."

Aventurine's 'cake cats' were charming little menaces who managed to draw blood within the first five minutes. They would grow up to be very capable warriors, indeed. He gently squished the toe beans of the most violent cat, Poker, who accepted it with grace and churring happily from his affections, only to bite his hand twenty seconds later like an overly enthusiastic hole puncher. Her tail was curled with joy, lying over his hand with idle possessiveness.

"She isn't usually so… aggressive." Aventurine noted as he stood to the side, observing. Poker's siblings crowded around his ankle, nearly tripping him up several times as he gave Phainon a glass of water.

"Little cretins," the golden-haired man muttered, "I am so telling on you to Ratio." He snickered at their lamenting yowls, grabbing them into his arms with an overly dramatic apology for his harsh threat.

"Does Ratio come here often?"

"He comes here for the cats. They get angsty when he leaves them for too long." Aventurine replied, eyes narrowing in a silent threat to drop the subject. Phainon had a suspicion that it weren't only the cats who missed him.

"Well, thanks for inviting me over. Is there anything I can do for you?"

Aventurine waved off his offer. "No need. Anyway, the guest bedrooms are on the second floor, pick whichever one you want. You got all you need for the night? Good, good, I'll be heading up then."

With all three cats clinging onto him, Aventurine left the room. Just before leaving, he called out to him. "Goodnight, Phainon."

"Night!"

With that last word, he left. His words were delivered with a hesitance that betrayed his age, his tongue curling over the wish with noticeable unfamiliarity, especially as his voice and tone were smoother than butter and impenetrable as Lady Aglaea's countenance. Phainon had the feeling that there hadn't been many people for him to say goodnight to for a long, long time.

Aventurine: Hah, are you not going to answer my question? Ah well, I'm getting the impression that the next activity was something you wanted to do and decided to use Phainon and I as an excuse to indulge.

Aventurine: Not going to confirm or deny that, too?

Aventurine: Goodnight, Doc.

Ratio: Goodnight, you foolish gambler.

Phainon spent the night reminiscing and sorting out all of the things he witnessed — nobody knows what a dromas is, but they have even stranger animals! Like a flamingo. Also, there are soooo many mass extinction events, I know that's unsurprising, but still! — he wanted to share with his loved ones later on his notes app. In the end, it was even more descriptive than his usual notes for his debate club. The network connecting Amphoreus to the wider galaxy was still underway, knocking into unforeseen complications, and by that, he meant the whole planet initially being just lines and lines of coding was quite an annoyance due to some technical issues he currently did not understand. If it weren't for that, Phainon would have been constantly texting his friends instead of living in the present and trying to actually relax. The night dragged on, and the sun rose promptly at 5 A.M. It still felt as if the night, new in its darkness, flashed in a blink. Phainon hadn't slept, but it wasn’t as if he needed it.

Aventurine woke up at 7:30. Phainon heard the distant yowl of one of the cat cakes (it sounded like Poker, but her siblings weren't as vocal as here, so he was not entirely sure what their battle cries sounded like) and then rushed apologies; Aventurine seemed to be a clumsy man in the morning.

The car ride to the spa — which did have baths, how lucky! — was nothing special, apart from maybe Aventurine occasionally resting his head on Ratio as he was still tired, only stopping when that nearly got them in a car crash. (Was the silence from Ratio whilst driving not a product of his general introverted nature, but perhaps… he was bad at driving and needed to focus?)

When Phainon asked this, Ratio only replied, "I need to focus because there are inept fools who somehow passed their driving tests on every single road."

Aventurine snickered at him.

They had split up to wander around the facility to choose what they would prefer. Before sauntering into the pedicure section, Aventurine had advised him to take the full-body massage.

However, it was obvious that Aventurine had failed to calculate one single thing: Phainon had somehow taken a page out of Mydei's tits book by gaining a nigh indestructible body that soaked up damage like a sponge. Now, in his quest to go Super Saiyan (according to Stelle. Nobody knew what she meant), this was a very good feature. But now? Not so much.

"I'm so sorry," the poor masseuse sobbed, forgetting to stop the entire vial of oil pouring down his back in her despair. It joined her tears on the floor. "There's— there's nothing I can do for you. I've never seen such tense knots in my life! Sir, are you okay?!"

Before he could respond, her eyes suddenly regained their light, hidden strength finally blooming within when everything was, quite frankly, going to shit.

"I cannot do anything for you anymore, sir." She whispered, not a trace of emotion in her tear-stained voice. "But I know someone who can. Please…excuse me."

She left the room with her head raised high, shoulders set with grim determination, the spirit of the indomitable human spirit glowing within so clearly Phainon could nearly taste the golden aura. He gave her his most approving nod, one forged in blood and strife. She nodded back, cool and collected.

"GRAMMY!" She yelled out, her call to arms rendering a shiver down his spine. The spa turned silent, every atom turning to attention now that the reinforcements, a one-grandma army was summoned. His intuition quaked; he was going to need faith, hope and pixie dust and his love for his friends and Mydei and Mydei's pectorals in his heart.

Grammy crept out of the shadows like the wraiths of a bygone era, or perhaps like the Black Tide itself, insurmountable and quiet as death itself.

"If you survive, young boy," Grammy croaked out, voice as ancient and worn down as the sand coating Pier Point. Her posture of steel indicated her true strength. "You may call me Grammy afterwards. Now, prove to me that your case was worth my grandchild getting me out of the break room."

As Phainon had been raised to utilise proper respect when speaking to one's elders, he said, "Yes, Madam."

The other worker silently witnessed his trial, hands clasped in prayer. "Please, do not mind me; I have much to learn still."

Grammy cracked her gnarled knuckles, wiser and older than the Grove of Epiphany itself, and then set her tiny shoulders into a king's resting position. Behind her thick lenses, she scanned his shoulders and back, finding no blemishes apart from severe emotional scars, knots hard enough to crack steel and the possibility of future scoliosis if she didn't fix his back right then and there.

"Please be gentle," Phainon begged quietly, dread writhing within him; not even Nanook or that bitch Lygus had ever scared him right down to the core of his heart, locked behind layers and layers of good humour, trauma, deflection, people pleasing, trauma, wrath and hope.

Grammy narrowed her hazy brown eyes at him. "If you wanted gentle," she spat out, "you should've gone to your boyfriend, bitch boy."

With those final words, Phainon closed his eyes and dreamt of Aedes Elysiae. Her hands found his weak spots and relentlessly beat them up. Wheat fields, the perfectly blue sky, his Ma's cooking, smoke rising from the hearth. Grammy held his shoulders down and went to town. He felt nothing but the agony of settled stress being punted out by some little old woman's hands. His torso seized about, a dying fish placed on that butcher's table.

"You cannot run away from here, nor can you continue to run away from the present." She hissed out. "You've achieved it all, haven't you? Your world is rescued by the Nameless Hero, the Deliver, the Dawn-Denied Khaslana. You are finally free. But you don't know what to do with yourself now that the future has finally been unlocked."

She pressed her palms into his shoulder blades and pushed, pressure exiting with a dying whimper. "Admit it: that small part of yourself wishes you could go back to those recurrent cycles — you knew exactly what would await. By having no future, you did not have to grow, grow past your title of Deliverer and the young boy nestled deep within. You could see your home again, even if only for a nostalgic-dimmed heartbeat. You didn't have to face yourself and your friends, who will grow out of the need to keep you close, who will have to decide whether they want you in your life. You didn't have to take the true, meaningful steps into fully accepting his love."

Trussed up like a damn turkey, Phainon could only take the verbal slaughtering.

"Even now, you look into the mirror and find yourself lacking. But I promise you, young boy, you will find the strength to grow beyond the shadow of those endless cycles."

She struck down on his tenth thoracic vertebra.

It cracked wetly, like Mydei #2's sole weak point when Phainon missed the sweet spot at first and had to spend the next few minutes hacking and cleaving at his lover's poor, abused spine as he couldn't see through the tears. Sorry, Cycle 2's Mydei, he thought grimly, I now truly understand your agony. May we meet again where the West Wind blows—

She struck down again, and something gave way.

His body seized up, ghosts and vague impressions of the coreflames he'd once accumulated over 33 million epochs blazing. His unfamiliar vessel surged with inhuman power, gold scars melting rivers through charred limbs, chest burning burning burning—

“Get that ratty thing off my operating table,” she snarled, and Khaslana nearly ripped the remaining wing off in his haste to 'yeet' it off the table.

"Sorry, Ma'am." He gasped out, wing futilely fluttering as he was pinned down.

When Aventurine had said full-body massage, he meant it. Grammy probably scraped a whole layer of dead akin off his body by the end of it during her hellish ministrations.

Khaslana heaved a mighty sob that shocked the still water surrounding his heart; he thought of his loved ones and their ghosts that haunted him even when they gave him their blessings.

"But— but how can I move one, I'm so sick—so sick of feeling like I'm stuck rolling up a boulder up an impossible mountain where the only thing I'm in control of is how quickly I push it up."

She nodded sagely, her massaging now softer as the past shed like a snake's scales. "You may find others during your journey, such as the itsy bitsy spider and Kate Bush."

"W—Who?"

"Never mind, love. You have friends to rely on. Your burden is nigh incomprehensible, but the love stayed, no? Well, to be frank, that burden is incomprehensible to you right now, as you've never had the time nor the energy to truly process your overwhelming grief. Remember this, young boy, your friends want you to share your feelings, especially when they are messy or disgusting. Stop holding it in, or I will personally shatter your tenth thoracic vertebra. After all, you would do the same thing for yourself, no?"

Phainon sniffled. "Do you have any more sage advice, Grammy?"

"Your wish is shit. Live for yourself from now on. Go wear those ugly ass clothes and do karaoke or some shit with your newest friends."

The sun, weakened and battered, finally started to rise, not with agony or rage, but the quiet, burgeoning hope of a new beginning, a true dawn rising, not just for Amphoreus, but for him as well.

"Thank you," he whispered, "but how do you know all of this…?"

She passed him a towel. "That doesn't matter — go to the baths."

Back in his mortal form and lighter than a feather, Phainon floated to the bathhouse, untethered by worldly desires (apart from his lover's pectorals, of course, as a treat) and strife. His skin was smoother than a baby's, and he felt every atom of air brushing against new skin. He shivered and continued his journey onwards.

By a stroke of fortune, he found his two companions bathing in the same spot, Aventurine sinking down until only his face was visible and Ratio with his entire upper torso shown. He noted that the scholar had impressive pectorals and biceps for such a nerd. Aventurine also thought the same, as his eyes were glued onto his bust. Despite being the second-most paranoid, constantly aware-of-their-surroundings blond Phainon had ever personally met, Aventurine did not notice him at all, far too engrossed by the heaving badonkadonks in front of him until Phainon entered the baths, finding them nicely warm.

Ratio took in the bruises developing around his torso and the blood that dribbled out of his mouth, already crusting over.

"Did you happen to get into a fight with your masseuse?" Ratio questioned, already thinking of the salves Phainon might need. He paid no attention to the thirsty maniac beside him. Fondly, he thought of all those times he took Mydei out to the baths (and 'baths'), sometimes even twice a day if they were both free enough. He let that warmth soak his bones, then refocused.

"Yeah. Grammy got me good."

At that name, Aventurine finally twitched back into sentience. "Grammy's still here? Her descendants have been trying to get her to retire for, like, a century. Oh, damn, I can see that her … loving touch has left its impact."

"Have you ever gone head to head with Grammy?" Phainon ignored Ratio's incredulous look as he tried to work out whatever the fuck was going on.

"Yeah. She's the reason why I didn't go insane, like, fifteen years ago and still have a modicum of human decency, y'know?"

For a pure, golden minute, Phainon melted into the baths. They weren't nearly as opulent or had as many oils as the Hero's Baths in Okhema, but they were pretty good.

Phainon nodded thoughtfully to himself. "I think I might propose to Mydei."

Ratio's brows furrowed further; Aventurine 'ooooh'ed and gestured for him to keep going. After muttering about fools and idiots, Ratio escaped to the colder baths and held his head underneath the water, either testing out his lung capacity or drowning out their voices.

"It's like — I love him with all my heart, I really do, but I've never said anything about the true depths of my love, never even made the first move once over the course of 33550336 cycles—"

Here, Aventurine's ever-present smile wavered in confusion.

"He usually comes up to me, challenges me to a duel, and if I lose, he tells me that we're now romantic partners and if I refuse, I'll have to kill him in another duel. If I win the first time, he challenges me until he wins, but by then he moves to underhanded tactics like flexing his tits when he knows I really love them when we wrestle—"

Ratio was definitely trying to drown himself now, judging by the smothered screaming.

"— but I've never told him that I love him. Fucked up, isn't it? I can't say the words to him, but to you guys, I can somehow say it! But— but how can I propose to him when I've killed him 33550336 times over through his singular weak spot that he always trusts me with?!"

Aventurine's smile crumpled into mild despair. His weak, guttural cry of buddy, I think you need to go back to Grammy was duly noted, but Phainon carried on.

"But I've already told him about that, and he forgave me, but how can I forgive myself— oh, yes, Grammy told me what to do! I must move on. I cannot rewrite our past, but we can make love AND new memories that aren't shadowed by our cruel fates!"

He stood up, arms splayed in passion. "Oh, when I get back, I will cook him breakfast and ardently profess my love for him and desire to grow as a person and show him the depths of my love and admiration for his peerless body every single day. Until death or that fucker Nanook and his loser Emanators try to pull me away from his loving arms!"

So lost in his passionate speech that would give his speech at the Flamechase debate a run for its money, he only realised that Aventurine fled to take refuge in Ratio's loving bosom afterwards. Phainon smiled, knowing that his general state of mental unwellbeing had pushed them closer. Ah, young love truly was a sight to behold!
